title: Distributed caches
subtitle: One cache server is not enough. Learn how to spread keys over many, what each lost node costs you, and how to keep the copies honest.

c.v: On 22 February 2022, just after 6 a.m. Pacific time, Slack users started to have trouble connecting. Responders found very high load on one part of the database.

One query made this much worse. When a client started, it loaded the members of every group direct message the user was in. That data was sharded by user, so "even one channel missing from cache" meant a query on every shard. Database load grew "superlinearly" as misses grew. Most of those queries timed out, so the cache could not fill again.
Pausing the upgrade early on did not help. Slack had to limit how many clients could start. It also changed the query to read only the missing data.
Mcrib worked as designed. It was so fast at replacing nodes that the cache emptied faster than it could refill.

A distributed cache is many cache servers that act like one big cache. You need one when a single server cannot hold the data your app reads, cannot serve the request rate, or would hurt too much if it died.

Your database is sized for the misses, not for the full traffic. The hit rate is a capacity number. Anything that empties part of the cache (a lost node, a deploy, a new region) sends a sudden wave of load to your database.
Why one node is not enough
In 2013, Facebook ran hundreds of Memcached servers in each cluster, to take load off its databases. One popular page fetched 521 different cached items on average.
So one request can touch many cache servers. Once you have many nodes, every app server needs a rule that maps a key to a node.
The app hashes the key itself, usually with consistent hashing. There is no extra hop. But every client, in every language, must use the same hash and the same server list.
The app talks to a router, and the router picks the node. Mcrouter is "a memcached protocol router". Its README says it handles "almost 5 billion requests per second at peak".

A plain Memcached pool keeps no copies. A new node on the ring takes over about 1/(N + 1) of the keys, and those keys simply miss. A dead or replaced node loses all its keys. With 10 nodes, and keys and traffic spread evenly, losing one costs you about a tenth of your hits. That is what happened to Slack, one node at a time.

Facebook chose not to rehash a dead server's keys over the others. One key can be 20% of a server's requests, so the server that takes it over may fall over too. Instead, failed requests go to a small spare pool called Gutter, about 1% of the servers. Its entries expire quickly.

Facebook copies some keys to several servers in a pool. In its example, each request needs all 100 keys. Splitting them over two servers still sends every request to both. Copying them halves the load on each. Every write must then delete every copy.

Keeping the cache in step with the database
Facebook updates the database, then deletes the key from the cache. It deletes, not updates, because a delete is
Deleting still leaves a race. Step through it.

Facebook calls this a "stale set". Its fix is a lease: a 64-bit token the cache gives a client on a miss. The client must show the token to set the value. A delete cancels the token, so a late set with an old value is rejected.
To reach other clusters, Facebook does not rely on web servers to send deletes. A daemon called mcsqueal reads the SQL each database commits and sends the deletes to the caches.
Because deletes live in the database log, lost ones can be replayed. Mcsqueal also runs on the
databases in other regions. Each one sends a delete only when the change reaches its own database. So a reader there is less likely to put old data back in the cache.

A new or rebuilt cache cluster has a very poor hit rate. Facebook lets a cold cluster read misses from a warm cluster, not the database. That brings it back to full capacity "in a few hours instead of a few days".
To avoid a race, deletes in the cold cluster block new adds for two seconds.
Mcrouter offers this as WarmUpRoute. Gets try the cold node first and fall back to the warm one.
If you have no warm copy, let traffic in slowly, as Slack did.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: "If we lose one cache node, or a whole cluster, how much extra load hits the database?"
Make misses cheap. A large part of Slack's problem was a miss that queried every shard.
Limit how fast nodes are replaced or flushed. Fast churn empties the cache faster than misses refill it.
Chart hit rate, evictions and the top keys per node, next to database load.
Write down which data may be stale and for how long. That decides between delete, leases and near caches.
Plan warm-up before a migration, a new region or a full restart.
"Here is our cache-aside code. Find every place that sets a cache value after a database read. Show me the race with a concurrent write, and add a version check."
"Write a script that replays 1 hour of our key access log against an LRU cache of 4, 8 and 16 GB. Print the hit rate for each size."
"Add a near cache for these 20 keys with a 5-second maximum TTL, Redis client tracking, and a flush when the tracking connection drops."
Every local copy has a maximum TTL and a memory limit.
The replay test uses real, skewed traffic. Uniform fake keys hide hot keys.
There is a limit on how many clients can start at once, for the day the cache is empty.

q.v: A Memcached pool uses consistent hashing over 10 nodes. One node dies and is replaced by an empty spare. What happens to the hit rate?

options.v: Nothing. The other nodes still have copies of its keys.
It drops by about one tenth, until the new node fills up from misses.
It drops to zero, because every key moves.

why.v: This pool keeps no copies. The keys that lived on the lost node now miss, and the other nine nodes keep theirs.

q.v: Why did Facebook send a failed server's traffic to a small Gutter pool, instead of rehashing it over the remaining servers?

options.v: Rehashing is too slow to compute.
A single hot key could overload whichever server took it over.
Gutter keeps data forever, so it never misses.

why.v: The paper says one key can be 20% of a server's requests. Moving it onto a busy server can start a chain of failures.

q.v: Reader A misses, reads v1 from the database, and is slow. Meanwhile writer B saves v2 and deletes the key. With leases, what happens when A tries to set v1?

options.v: The cache stores v1, and v2 is lost.
The cache rejects the set, because B's delete cancelled A's lease.
The cache waits for B to finish, then stores v1.

why.v: A delete cancels any lease on that key. A set with a cancelled lease is refused, so old data does not go back in.

q.v: Every request needs the same 100 small keys, and one server can hold them all but cannot serve the request rate. What helps most?

options.v: Split the 100 keys over more servers.
Copy all 100 keys to several servers, and send each request to one copy.
Switch the eviction policy from LRU to LFU.

why.v: Splitting means each request still visits every server. Copies let each server take a share of the requests.

q.v: You add a near cache in each app server. What must you also add?

options.v: A way to drop local copies when the data changes, plus a maximum TTL.
Nothing. Local copies cannot go stale.

why.v: A local copy goes stale when the data changes. You need invalidation messages, and a TTL as a safety net if they are lost.
